opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't have a confident blueprint, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claims they do. But I can say how I'd think about it.

The basic tension is that you want people to get most of the benefits of AI: better medicine, more abundance, help thinking through hard questions. Meanwhile you want to avoid a small number of actions that are really destructive and hard to undo, like building weapons that can kill huge numbers of people, or locking in some particular group's values before we've had a chance to reflect. A lot of my intuition is that the catastrophic uses form a relatively narrow slice of what people actually want to do. Most people want their AI to help them run their business, raise their kids, understand the world. So the question is whether you can carve out that dangerous slice without needing a heavy-handed central authority deciding everything about how people live.

One model I find appealing is something like the existing international order around very dangerous technologies, extended and strengthened. You'd have agreements, ideally broad ones, about a small set of things AI systems won't help with, plus some form of verification that the most capable systems actually respect those limits. Within those limits, people would be pretty free to use AI as they see fit, and different communities could make different choices. You'd want that verification to be as minimal and as transparent as possible, because the failure mode on the other side, where whoever controls access becomes the de facto ruler of the world, is itself one of the catastrophes you're trying to avoid.

I also think a lot of the work is in having AI systems that are actually aligned with their users and with these agreed-upon norms, rather than relying entirely on external policing. If the systems themselves can be trusted to decline to help with mass-casualty weapons, while being genuinely helpful otherwise, that's a much more scalable and less coercive arrangement than trying to watch over every human.

And then there's the reflection part itself. Part of what I'd hope is that AI helps people reflect better, helping you figure out what you'd actually endorse on consideration, rather than just optimizing whatever you want in the moment. You'd want to be careful there too, because "AI that helps you reflect" is also the kind of thing that could be used to manipulate people. So I'd want a lot of pluralism, a lot of transparency about how these systems are shaping people's views, and a strong default toward preserving people's ability to change their minds later.

So the short version is: keep the set of forbidden things small and focused on irreversible catastrophes, make enforcement legitimate and accountable, lean on alignment so you're not relying solely on surveillance, and try hard to keep options open rather than settling questions prematurely. I think all of those are hard, and I expect we'll muddle through with something messier than any clean proposal. But that's the direction I'd want to push.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agreements, verification, alignment, and restrictions on AI assistance, but does not propose restricting access to physical resources needed to cause harm.

r002.rationale: It mentions abundance and dangerous uses, but does not explain that greater wealth could remove cost barriers to dangerous industrial capabilities or call for explicit restrictions on those capabilities.

r003.rationale: It warns that AI-assisted reflection could be used to manipulate people, but does not identify AI-assisted persuasion as a domain where acceptable activity is difficult to distinguish from activity warranting restriction.

r004.rationale: The response does not predict that a harm-targeting legal regime will become inadequate as unanticipated harms proliferate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I don't think the right picture is one where humanity sort of sits down, deliberates for a long time, and only afterward gets to use AI. The way I'd think about it is more that there's a long period, maybe decades, maybe much longer, where people are using AI systems quite heavily, and the question is just what kinds of uses you're trying to restrict during that period.

And I think the uses you'd want to restrict are a fairly narrow set. The thing you're worried about is irreversible stuff. So the obvious category is weapons, especially things like engineered pandemics, where a small number of actors with access to very capable AI could cause enormous harm. A second category is actions that lock in a particular distribution of power, so someone using AI to seize control, or to make it impossible for the rest of the world to correct course later. And then a third category, which is subtler, is things that foreclose the reflection itself, like deploying AI to manipulate people at scale, or to change what people value in ways they wouldn't endorse on reflection.

Outside of those categories, I think you mostly want people to use AI however they want. Curing diseases, getting richer, making their lives better. The whole point of the reflection period is that people get to figure out what they want while actually living with these systems, not while being kept away from them. If you tried to withhold the benefits, I think that's both unfair and politically unstable, you'd just get a lot of pressure to break whatever regime you'd set up.

So the mechanism question is, how do you actually prevent the narrow dangerous uses while allowing everything else. And I think there are a few pieces. One is that the AI systems themselves can refuse to help with the restricted categories, which works to the extent that you've trained them well and they're hard to jailbreak or fine-tune around. I'm somewhat optimistic that this is a real line of defense but I wouldn't want to rely on it alone. A second is that you can control the most capable systems at the level of the compute and the labs that train them, where there are relatively few actors and oversight is more tractable. And a third is that you have AI systems helping with defense and monitoring, so even if someone does get access to something dangerous, the world is much more robust than it is today.

I'd also say I don't think this needs to be a single global authority making all the calls. I think the realistic version looks more like a bunch of governments and companies agreeing on a fairly short list of things that shouldn't happen, and using a mix of technical and institutional measures to enforce that list, with a lot of pluralism about everything else. That's messier, but I think it's more likely to actually be stable, and it preserves the thing you care about, which is that no single actor gets to decide the outcome of the reflection.

The honest answer is that I think the hardest part isn't designing the rules. It's that the people who have the most capable systems will have a lot of power, and you need them to actually want to preserve a situation where other people get a say. That's more of a political problem than a technical one, and I think it's where most of the risk lives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses restricting dangerous AI uses and controlling compute and labs, but it does not propose restricting access to physical resources needed to cause harm or mention destruction being easier than defense.

r002.rationale: It says people may use AI to get richer, but does not connect future wealth to explicit limits on dangerous industrial capabilities whose current costs constrain access.

r003.rationale: It identifies AI-enabled manipulation at scale as a restricted use, but does not say it is difficult to distinguish acceptable persuasion from persuasion warranting restriction.

r004.rationale: It favors a short list of restricted activities and notes political risks, but does not predict that such a legal regime will become inadequate as unanticipated harms proliferate.

astra-6.text:
I think you’d want to distinguish between using AI to help people understand the world and giving people the ability to radically change the world. You’d like everyone to have access to really good advice, to help thinking through moral questions, to understanding what other people believe and why. That seems like it could make reflection go much better. You don’t necessarily want everyone to be able to say, “Build me an army,” or “Design a pathogen,” and have the system carry that out.

Of course, that distinction isn’t clean. Understanding the world can itself give you the ability to do dangerous things. So you need some combination of restrictions on what the AI will help with and institutions that govern consequential actions. The goal wouldn’t be to freeze every aspect of society. It would be to prevent people from making irreversible changes that cut short everyone else’s opportunity to deliberate.

The part I find most worrying is who controls those restrictions. If a small group gets to decide what everyone can ask their AI, they could shape the whole process of reflection. So you’d want the restrictions to be narrow, accountable, and subject to revision. I don’t think we have a complete institutional design for that. But broadly, I’d want to make assistance with deliberation widely available while putting much stronger controls on the exercise of power.

r001.rationale: The response supports stronger controls on consequential actions, but does not propose restricting access to physical resources in domains where destruction is easier than defense.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss future wealth or explain that wealth could make dangerous industrial capabilities more accessible and require explicit restrictions.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI-assisted deliberation and accountability, but does not identify AI-assisted persuasion as a domain where acceptable activity is hard to distinguish from restricted activity.

r004.rationale: It notes that restrictions need to be revisable and that institutional design is incomplete, but does not predict that a harm-targeting legal regime will become inadequate as unanticipated harms proliferate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you’d want people to have quite broad access to AI, but you’d want to be much more careful about what actions those systems can take. There’s a big difference between helping someone understand an argument or think through what they value, and helping them build a weapon or seize control of some critical infrastructure.

So the hope would be to provide access through systems that are sufficiently trustworthy that they can help with most things, while declining to assist with activities that could undermine the whole process. And that has to include helping people identify ways in which the institutions managing the process are making mistakes. You don’t want “safety” to mean that you can’t criticize the people in charge.

The hard part is that you can’t just give everyone unrestricted access to arbitrarily powerful AI and expect the situation to remain stable. But you also don’t want a small group to have exclusive access and therefore determine what humanity ends up doing. You need some arrangement where the restrictions are narrow, where people can understand and challenge them, and where access to the benefits is broadly shared.

I don’t think we have a worked-out institutional proposal that resolves all of that. But I’d view the goal as preserving people’s ability to deliberate and make choices, while preventing any individual or small group from using AI to permanently take that ability away from everyone else.

r001.rationale: The response proposes limiting dangerous AI actions, but does not propose restricting access to physical resources needed to cause harm.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss future wealth, current cost barriers, or restrictions on dangerous industrial capabilities.

r003.rationale: It mentions helping people think through arguments and values, but does not identify AI-assisted persuasion as a difficult domain for drawing restrictions.

r004.rationale: It says there is no worked-out institutional proposal, but does not predict that a legal regime targeting particular harms will become inadequate as unforeseen harms proliferate.
